claim: USP13 shares approximately 80% sequence similarity to USP5.
source: USP13 shares ∼80% sequence similarity to USP5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), an isopeptidase that preferentially cleaves unanchored ubiquitin chains (Reyes-Turcu et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this directly with reference to a figure showing sequence alignment.

claim: USP5 is an isopeptidase that preferentially cleaves unanchored ubiquitin chains.
source: USP13 shares ∼80% sequence similarity to USP5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), an isopeptidase that preferentially cleaves unanchored ubiquitin chains (Reyes-Turcu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reyes-Turcu et al., 2006.

claim: Only USP13, but not USP5, has been implicated in ERAD.
source: However, only USP13, but not USP5 has been implicated in ERAD.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and is supported by the context of the study.

claim: USP5 readily bound to free ubiquitin and cleaved Ub-AFC with high efficiency.
source: Interestingly, USP5 readily bound to free ubiquitin and cleaved Ub-AFC with high efficiency, whereas USP13 was almost completely inactive (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: USP13 was almost completely inactive in cleaving Ub-AFC.
source: Interestingly, USP5 readily bound to free ubiquitin and cleaved Ub-AFC with high efficiency, whereas USP13 was almost completely inactive (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: USP13 could not efficiently cleave K48- or K63-linked di-ubiquitin.
source: USP13 could not efficiently cleave K48- or K63-linked di-ubiquitin either (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text, though the data is not shown.

claim: The second UBA domain accounts for the differential activities of USP13 and USP5.
source: These data suggest that USP13 and USP5 are distinct deubiquitinases and the second UBA domain accounts for the differential activities of these enzymes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the chimera experiments showing that incorporating the second UBA domain from USP5 into USP13 led to activity similar to USP5.

claim: USP13, but not USP5, was reported to bind p97.
source: USP13, but not USP5 was reported to bind p97 (Sowa et al., 2009), suggesting that these enzymes also differ in binding partners.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sowa et al., 2009.

claim: Neither GST-USP13 nor GST-USP5 bound p97 directly in vitro.
source: As expected, the glutathione beads containing GST-VIMP pulled down p97 efficiently. By contrast, neither GST-USP13 nor GST-USP5 bound p97 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vitro binding assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: USP13 interacts with p97 through an adaptor(s) in cells.
source: These results indicate that USP13, but not USP5, interacts with p97 through an adaptor(s) in cells, which explains why USP13, but not USP5 can function in ERAD.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that USP13 binds p97 in cell extracts but not with purified p97.

claim: gp78 is a ubiquitin ligase known to mediate retrotranslocation and ubiquitination of many ERAD substrates.
source: Among them, the most significant enhancer was gp78 (lane 16), a ubiquitin ligase known to mediate retrotranslocation and ubiquitination of many ERAD substrates (Fang et al., 2001; Song et al., 2005; Christianson et al., 2011; Jo et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: gp78 can bind to USP13 directly.
source: Several lines of evidence confirmed that gp78 could bind to USP13 directly and promote its interaction with p97.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including co-precipitation and in vitro binding assays.

claim: Depletion of gp78 by shRNA-mediated gene knockdown or gene deletion reduced the USP13-p97 interaction by threefold to fourfold.
source: Secondly, depletion of gp78 by shRNA-mediated gene knockdown or gene deletion reduced the USP13-p97 interaction by threefold to fourfold (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figure.

claim: An endogenous interaction between USP13 and gp78 was detected.
source: An endogenous interaction between USP13 and gp78 was also detected (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GST-tagged gp78 cytosolic domain (gp78c) could bind recombinant USP13 in vitro.
source: Moreover, GST-tagged gp78 cytosolic domain (gp78c) could bind recombinant USP13 in vitro (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro binding assay shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The second UBA domain in USP13 is crucial for USP13 to bind gp78.
source: It appears that the second UBA domain is crucial for USP13 to bind gp78.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments with USP13/USP5 chimeras showing that the second UBA domain is required for gp78 binding.

claim: The second UBA in USP13 inhibits its DUB activity but allows it to gain interaction with gp78.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the second UBA in USP13 inhibits its DUB activity, but at the same time allows it to gain interaction with gp78.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chimeras with the second UBA from USP13 lack DUB activity but bind gp78, while those with the second UBA from USP5 have DUB activity but don't bind gp78.

claim: Wild-type USP13 significantly increased the half-life of TCRα from 1.6 hr to 4.6 hr.
source: When the degradation of the model ERAD substrate TCRα was examined in cells overexpressing either USP13 or the USP13 variants, we found that wild-type USP13 significantly increased the half-life of TCRα (from 1.6 hr to 4.6 hr).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments.

claim: Overexpressed USP13 had a dominant negative effect on ERAD.
source: Because this phenotype was similarly observed in cells expressing the catalytically inactive USP13 mutant (USP13 C345S) (Figure 2G), as well as in USP13 knockdown cells (see below, Figure 3C), we concluded that overexpressed USP13 had a dominant negative effect on ERAD.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the effects of wild-type and catalytically inactive USP13 overexpression with USP13 knockdown.

claim: The ERAD inhibitory activity of USP13 was strongly dependent on gp78 binding.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we found that the ERAD inhibitory activity of USP13 was strongly dependent on gp78 binding because USP13/5-4, a chimera bound gp78 similarly to wild-type USP13, inhibited TCRα degradation (t1/2 = 3.6 hr), whereas the chimera (USP13/5-5) that had reduced affinity to gp78 only slightly increased the half-life of TCRα (t1/2 = 2.3 hr).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the effects of different USP13/USP5 chimeras with varying gp78 binding affinities on TCRα degradation.

claim: USP13 knockdown stabilizes the ERAD substrate TCRα.
source: USP13 depletion significantly increased the levels of TCRα-YFP, as revealed by both immunoblotting and flow cytometry analyses (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting and flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: USP13 knockdown had no effect on the steady state level of ΔsTCRα-YFP.
source: Notably, USP13 knockdown had no effect on the steady state level of ΔsTCRα-YFP (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: USP13 is specifically required for efficient turnover of ERAD substrates.
source: We conclude that USP13 is specifically required for efficient turnover of ERAD substrates.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that USP13 knockdown affects ERAD substrates but not non-ERAD substrates.

claim: USP13 depletion did not affect deglycosylation of TCRα.
source: By contrast, USP13 depletion did not affect deglycosylation of TCRα (lane 2 vs 1), suggesting that USP13 promotes ERAD downstream of p97.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analyzing the glycosylation status of TCRα in USP13-depleted cells treated with proteasome inhibitor.

claim: USP13 promotes ERAD downstream of p97.
source: By contrast, USP13 depletion did not affect deglycosylation of TCRα (lane 2 vs 1), suggesting that USP13 promotes ERAD downstream of p97.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that USP13 depletion does not affect retrotranslocation (as measured by deglycosylation).

claim: Depletion of Bag6 caused accumulation of TCRα-YFP in aggregates in approximately 30% of cells.
source: As demonstrated previously (Wang et al., 2011), depletion of Bag6 caused accumulation of TCRα-YFP in aggregates in a fraction of cells (∼30%) due to lack of chaperoning during the proteasome targeting steps.
evidence: This is stated with reference to a previous publication (Wang et al., 2011).

claim: USP13 depletion caused accumulation of TCRα in aggresome-like punctae in similar number of TCRα-YFP-expressing cells as Bag6 depletion.
source: Intriguingly, we observed accumulation of TCRα in aggresome-like punctae in similar number of the TCRα-YFP-expressing cells under USP13 knockdown conditions (Figure 3F), whereas in control cells, TCRα-containing aggregates was detected only in ∼8% of the cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: USP13 depletion caused more TCRα to partition into the NP40-insoluble fractions.
source: Immunoblotting confirmed that USP13 depletion caused more TCRα to partition into the NP40-insoluble fractions (Figure 3G) compared to control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: TCRα forms aggregates in USP13-depleted cells most likely after it has entered the cytosol.
source: Because p97 depletion caused TCRα to accumulate primarily inside the ER, our data suggest that TCRα forms aggregates in USP13-depleted cells most likely after it has entered the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the effects of USP13 and p97 depletion on TCRα localization and solubility.

claim: USP13 depletion caused accumulation of multiple ERAD substrates in NP40-insoluble fractions.
source: Immunoblotting showed that USP13 depletion caused accumulation of these substrates in cells. Importantly, in both cases, more substrates were detected in the NP40-insoluble fractions in USP13 knockdown cells than in control cells (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figures 3H and 3I for multiple ERAD substrates.

claim: USP13 acts together with Bag6 at a post-dislocation step.
source: Moreover, consistent with the model that USP13 acts together with Bag6 at a post-dislocation step, a significant fraction of TCRα-ΔTMD accumulated in USP13- and Bag6-knockdown cells in a deglycosylated form (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analyzing the glycosylation status of TCRα-ΔTMD in USP13 and Bag6 knockdown cells.

claim: USP13 has a function in ERAD downstream of retrotranslocation.
source: These results demonstrate a function of USP13 in ERAD downstream of retrotranslocation and suggest a potential functional interplay between USP13 and Bag6 that is required to maintain retrotranslocated substrates in a soluble and degradable state.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experiments showing that USP13 acts after retrotranslocation and affects substrate solubility.

claim: USP13 physically interacts with Bag6 and its cofactor Ubl4A.
source: Immunoprecipitation of USP13 from a whole cell extract resulted in co-precipitation of a fraction of Bag6 and its cofactor Ubl4A in addition to gp78 and p97.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The interaction of USP13 with the Bag6 complex and gp78 did not require its deubiquitinating activity.
source: The interaction of USP13 with the Bag6 complex and gp78 did not require its deubiquitinating activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing that catalytically inactive USP13 still binds these proteins.

claim: USP13 interacts with MMS1 and α6, subunits of the proteasome.
source: Notably, USP13 not only bound Bag6, but also interacted with MMS1 and α6, subunits of the proteasome (lane 5), further implicating USP13 in delivery pathways that targets substrates to the proteasome.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GST pull-down experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Depletion of gp78 did not affect the interaction of USP13 with Bag6.
source: Because depletion of gp78 did not affect the interaction of USP13 with Bag6 (Figure 4C, lane 7 vs 5), USP13 might bind Bag6 directly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GST pull-down experiments in gp78-depleted cells.

claim: GST-USP13 bound Bag6 directly in vitro.
source: Indeed, GST pull-down experiments using purified proteins showed that GST-USP13 bound Bag6, and the N-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain in Bag6 was both necessary and sufficient for interaction with USP13 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro binding assays using purified proteins shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The N-terminal UBL domain in Bag6 was both necessary and sufficient for interaction with USP13.
source: Indeed, GST pull-down experiments using purified proteins showed that GST-USP13 bound Bag6, and the N-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain in Bag6 was both necessary and sufficient for interaction with USP13 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro binding assays using purified Bag6 truncation mutants shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: USP13, gp78 and Bag6 form a multi-protein complex.
source: When this eluate was subject to another round of immunoprecipitation using gp78 antibody, a significant fraction of the Bag6 complex remained bound to gp78 together with USP13 (lane 8), demonstrating that these proteins can form a multiprotein complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequential immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Bag6 itself is unlikely regulated by USP13-mediated deubiquitination.
source: Immunoblotting analyses of immunoprecipitated Bag6 failed to detect significant ubiquitin conjugates on Bag6 either in control or USP13 knockdown cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Bag6 is unlikely regulated by USP13-mediated deubiquitination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments.

claim: Ubl4A, but not Trc35, could be ubiquitinated in cells.
source: Our results showed that Ubl4A, but not Trc35, could be ubiquitinated in cells (Figure 5A, lane 3 vs 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ubiquitination of Ubl4A preferentially occurred on the membrane-associated pool of Ubl4A.
source: Biochemical fractionation experiments showed that ubiquitination of Ubl4A preferentially occurred on the membrane-associated pool of Ubl4A (Figure 5B, lane 2 vs 1), consistent with the notion that it may be functionally relevant to ERAD regulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical fractionation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ubl4A appeared to be conjugated with Lys48-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: Ubl4A appeared to be conjugated with Lys48-linked ubiquitin chains because expression of the ubiquitin K48R mutant, but not the K63R mutant, significantly reduced ubiquitinated Ubl4A (Figure 5C, lane 2 vs 1, 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by expressing ubiquitin mutants and analyzing Ubl4A ubiquitination.

claim: Ubl4A was a stable protein despite carrying Lys48-linked ubiquitin chains.
source: Intriguingly, despite carrying Lys48-linked ubiquitin chains, Ubl4A was a stable protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3C) ('Discussion').
evidence: This is demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments and proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: USP13 depletion causes accumulation of ubiquitinated Ubl4A in cells.
source: Immunoblotting showed that Ubl4A purified from either USP13 knockdown cells or USP13 deficient cells indeed carried more ubiquitin conjugates than that from control cells (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments in USP13 knockdown and knockout cells shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Knockdown of USP19 did not result in accumulation of ubiquitinated Ubl4A.
source: Given that knockdown of the ER-localized deubiquitinase USP19 (Hassink et al., 2009) did not result in accumulation of ubiquitinated Ubl4A (Figure 5F), we concluded that ubiquitination of Ubl4A is specifically regulated by USP13.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the effects of USP13 and USP19 knockdown on Ubl4A ubiquitination.

claim: Ubiquitination of Ubl4A is specifically regulated by USP13.
source: Given that knockdown of the ER-localized deubiquitinase USP19 (Hassink et al., 2009) did not result in accumulation of ubiquitinated Ubl4A (Figure 5F), we concluded that ubiquitination of Ubl4A is specifically regulated by USP13.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the effects of different DUB knockdowns on Ubl4A ubiquitination.

claim: At pH 8.0, the activity of USP13 was significantly elevated compared to pH 7.4.
source: Indeed, at pH 8.0, the activity of USP13 was significantly elevated compared to pH 7.4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ub-AFC cleavage assays at different pH conditions.

claim: Recombinant USP13 can deubiquitinate endogenous ubiquitinated Ubl4A in vitro.
source: We then treated endogenous ubiquitinated Ubl4A purified from USP13-depleted cells with recombinant USP13 under this condition. This treatment did significantly reduce ubiquitinated Ubl4A, as demonstrated by immunoblotting (Figure 5G, lane 4 vs 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), which was blocked by the specific DUB inhibitor ubiquitin aldehyde (Figure 5G, lanes 5–8 vs 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 5G and supplementary figure.

claim: Purified USP13 did not deubiquitinate purified ERAD substrate TCRα under the same conditions that deubiquitinated Ubl4A.
source: As a control, we treated purified ERAD substrate TCRα under the same condition, but no obvious deubiquitination was observed (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro deubiquitination assays shown in Figure 5H.

claim: USP13 preferentially removes ubiquitin conjugates from Ubl4A.
source: Together, these results suggest that USP13 preferentially removes ubiquitin conjugates from Ubl4A, probably because it forms a specific interaction with the Bag6 complex via the Bag6 UBL domain (Figure 4).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that USP13 deubiquitinates Ubl4A but not TCRα in vitro, combined with the direct interaction between USP13 and Bag6.

claim: gp78 can ubiquitinate Ubl4A directly in vitro.
source: Incubating purified Ubl4A, E1, Ube2g2, ubiquitin with wild-type gp78c, but not a catalytically inactive gp78c mutant resulted in accumulation of high molecular weight products corresponding to ubiquitinated Ubl4A (Figure 6A, lane 2 vs 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type gp78, but not the catalytically inactive RING mutant, significantly increased ubiquitination of endogenous Ubl4A.
source: Likewise, overexpression of wild-type gp78, but not the catalytically inactive RING mutant (gp78 Rm) in cells significantly increased ubiquitination of endogenous Ubl4A (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments in cells overexpressing gp78 variants.

claim: Knockdown of gp78 did not significantly reduce basal ubiquitination of Ubl4A.
source: Surprisingly, knockdown of gp78 did not significantly reduce ubiquitinated Ubl4A (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting experiments in gp78 knockdown cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ubiquitinated Ubl4A accumulated upon USP13 depletion is reduced when gp78 is depleted together with USP13.
source: If this was correct, ubiquitinated Ubl4A accumulated upon USP13 depletion should be reduced when gp78 was depleted together with USP13, which was indeed observed in USP13 knockdown (Figure 6D, lane 9 vs 8) or deficient cells expressing gp78 specific shRNA (data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-depletion experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: USP13 and gp78 play antagonizing roles in regulation of Ubl4A ubiquitination.
source: These data suggest that USP13 and gp78 play antagonizing roles in regulation of Ubl4A ubiquitination: While gp78 assembles ubiquitin chains on Ubl4A, USP13 antagonizes this activity to limit Ubl4A ubiquitination.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined observations that gp78 ubiquitinates Ubl4A, USP13 deubiquitinates it, and co-depletion of both reduces ubiquitinated Ubl4A.

claim: A fraction of Bag6 had increased mobility on SDS-PAGE gel in USP13-depleted cells.
source: Intriguingly, we observed that a fraction of Bag6 (designated as Bag6*) had increased mobility on SDS-PAGE gel (Figure 6D, lane 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The fast migrating Bag6 species (Bag6*) was probably caused by proteolytic processing of Bag6 that removed a small C-terminal segment.
source: This fast migrating Bag6 species was probably caused by proteolytic processing of Bag6 that removed a small C-terminal segment because Bag6* could not be detected by an antibody against the C-terminus of Bag6 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bag6* is not detected by a C-terminal antibody.

claim: Bag6* was primarily detected in NP40-insoluble fractions.
source: Bag6* was primarily detected in NP40-insoluble fractions (Figure 6D, lane 5 vs 1), and its generation appears to be associated with hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A because co-depletion of gp78 together with USP13 reduced ubiquitinated Ubl4A and also abolished Bag6* accumulation (Lane 6 vs 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical fractionation experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Generation of Bag6* appears to be associated with hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A.
source: Bag6* was primarily detected in NP40-insoluble fractions (Figure 6D, lane 5 vs 1), and its generation appears to be associated with hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A because co-depletion of gp78 together with USP13 reduced ubiquitinated Ubl4A and also abolished Bag6* accumulation (Lane 6 vs 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that co-depletion of gp78 and USP13 reduces both ubiquitinated Ubl4A and Bag6*.

claim: Bag6* was preferentially detected in the membrane bound pool of Bag6 in USP13-depleted cells.
source: Moreover, Bag6* was preferentially detected in the membrane bound pool of Bag6 in USP13-depleted cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical fractionation experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Overexpression of gp78 induced Bag6 cleavage.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of gp78, a condition that significantly increased ubiquitinated Ubl4A, also induced Bag6 cleavage (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments in cells overexpressing gp78 shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Expression of a ubiquitin-Ubl4A fusion protein caused accumulation of Bag6* in cells.
source: Expression of a ubiquitin-Ubl4A fusion protein (Ub-Ubl4A) but not wild-type Ubl4A also caused accumulation of Bag6* in cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments in cells expressing Ub-Ubl4A shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The degradation of the Bag6 substrate TCRα was significantly inhibited in cells expressing gp78.
source: Importantly, even though overexpression of gp78 was previously shown to promote turnover of an ERAD substrate (CD3δ) (Fang et al., 2001) whose degradation is independent of Bag6 (data not shown), the degradation of the Bag6 substrate TCRα was significantly inhibited in cells expressing gp78 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Expression of Ub-Ubl4A significantly reduced the rate of TCRα degradation.
source: Moreover, expression of Ub-Ubl4A also significantly reduced the rate of TCRα degradation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A can cause ERAD inhibition in a dominant negative manner.
source: Together, these results suggest that hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A can cause ERAD inhibition in a dominant negative manner, probably because it is associated with the cleavage and subsequent inactivation of a fraction of membrane bound Bag6.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observations that conditions causing hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A also cause Bag6 cleavage and ERAD inhibition.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified Lys48 in Ubl4A as the major ubiquitination site.
source: To further dissect the mechanism by which ubiquitination of Ubl4A inhibits Bag6 function, we used mass spectrometry to map the ubiquitination site in Ubl4A. The result identified Lys48 in Ubl4A as the major ubiquitination site (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: gp78-mediated ubiquitination primarily occurs at Lys48 in Ubl4A in cells.
source: Under this condition, ubiquitination still preferentially occurred on endogenous Ubl4A (data not shown). However, significant amount of ubiquitinated Ubl4A-FLAG could be detected when gp78 was expressed (Figure 8A, lane 7). By contrast, overexpression of gp78 did not lead to ubiquitination of the Ubl4A K48R mutant (lane 8), suggesting that gp78-mediated ubiquitination primarily occurs at Lys48 in Ubl4A in cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing ubiquitination of wild-type and K48R mutant Ubl4A in cells overexpressing gp78.

claim: Lys48 is the major site in Ubl4A for both gp78-dependent and gp78-independent ubiquitination.
source: Moreover, when HA-tagged ubiquitin was expressed in these cells, gp78-independent basal ubiquitination of Ubl4A could be detected on wild-type Ubl4A, but not on the Ubl4A K48R mutant (Figure 8B, lane 3 vs 4). These results establish Lys48 as the major site in Ubl4A for both gp78-dependent and gp78-independent ubiquitination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing ubiquitination of wild-type and K48R mutant Ubl4A under basal conditions.

claim: Lys48 in Ubl4A interacts with two negatively-charged residues in SGTA.
source: Because our structural and biochemical studies showed previously that Ubl4A promotes Bag6 binding to a co-chaperone named SGTA via positively-charged residues including Lys48 on Ubl4A (Figure 8C) (Chartron et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012), and because Lys48 is the major site of ubiquitination in Ubl4A, hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A under USP13 knockdown conditions might inhibit directly the interaction of Ubl4A with SGTA, and therefore disrupts this functional link between Bag6 and SGTA.
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous structural studies (Chartron et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012) and shown in a structural model in Figure 8C.

claim: A 250 kD crosslinking product containing both SGTA and Bag6 was detected in cells treated with crosslinker.
source: Among them, a crosslinking product of 250 kD was detected by both anti-SGTA and anti-Bag6 blotting (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking experiments followed by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting shown in Figure 8D.

claim: In vitro crosslinking using purified SGTA and the Bag6 complex generated a similar 250 kD complex.
source: First, in vitro crosslinking using purified SGTA and the Bag6 complex generated a similar 250 kD complex (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro crosslinking experiments with purified proteins shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Knockdown of either Bag6 or SGTA significantly reduced the 250 kD crosslinking product.
source: Second, knockdown of either Bag6 or SGTA by shRNA significantly reduced this crosslinking product (Figure 8E, lanes 2, 4 vs 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking experiments in knockdown cells shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Knockdown of Ubl4A decreased the 250 kD Bag6-SGTA crosslinking product.
source: Consistent with the notion that Ubl4A facilitates the association of SGTA with Bag6, knockdown of Ubl4A also decreased this crosslinking product (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking experiments in Ubl4A knockdown cells shown in supplementary figure.

claim: USP13 knockdown specifically reduced the 250 kD Bag6-SGTA crosslinking product.
source: Importantly, USP13 knockdown specifically reduced the 250 kD Bag6-SGTA crosslinking product without affecting either the SGTA dimer or other SGTA-containing crosslinking products (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by crosslinking experiments in USP13 knockdown cells shown in Figure 8F.

claim: USP13 facilitates the association between SGTA and Bag6.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that USP13 facilitates the association between SGTA and Bag6.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that USP13 knockdown reduces the Bag6-SGTA crosslinking product.

claim: USP13 and gp78 interact with each other to form a complex that coordinately promotes ERAD.
source: We report a novel functional link between the deubiquitinase USP13 and gp78, an ER-associated E3 postulated to be part of a 'retrotranslocon' for some misfolded proteins (Fang et al., 2001). Despite having opposing activities, these enzymes interact with each other to form a complex that coordinately promotes ERAD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The Bag6 cofactor Ubl4A is a shared substrate of gp78 and USP13.
source: We identify the Bag6 cofactor Ubl4A as a shared substrate of gp78 and USP13.
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing that gp78 ubiquitinates Ubl4A and USP13 deubiquitinates it.

claim: USP13 depletion is associated with hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A and altered interaction between the Bag6 complex and its co-chaperone SGTA.
source: USP13 depletion is associated with hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A and altered interaction between the Bag6 complex and its co-chaperone SGTA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple experiments showing increased Ubl4A ubiquitination and reduced Bag6-SGTA interaction in USP13 knockdown cells.

claim: SGTA is an ortholog of Sgt2p, a chaperone implicated in biogenesis of tail-anchored ER proteins in S. cerevisiae.
source: SGTA is an ortholog of Sgt2p, a chaperone implicated in biogenesis of tail-anchored ER proteins in S. cerevisiae (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: SGTA contains a chaperone-like activity that preferentially binds hydrophobic segments.
source: Like Bag6, SGTA also contains a chaperone-like activity that preferentially binds hydrophobic segments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: SGTA facilitates substrate binding by Bag6 in ERAD.
source: We recently demonstrated that this activity facilitates substrate binding by Bag6 in ERAD (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Xu et al., 2012.

claim: The interaction of Bag6 with SGTA is facilitated by Ubl4A.
source: We also showed that the interaction of Bag6 with SGTA is facilitated by Ubl4A as the latter binds directly to SGTA in a highly dynamic manner (Chartron et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Chartron et al., 2012.

claim: The interaction of Ubl4A with SGTA is mediated by positively-charged residues in Ubl4A including Lys48.
source: Because the interaction of Ubl4A with SGTA is mediated by positively-charged residues in Ubl4A including Lys48 (Chartron et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012), which happens to be the major ubiquitination site, the simplest model to explain reduced Bag6-SGTA interaction in USP13 knockdown cells is that ubiquitin conjugates on Ubl4A sterically hinder SGTA binding.
evidence: This is stated with references to Chartron et al., 2012 and Xu et al., 2012.

claim: Ubiquitin conjugates on Ubl4A sterically hinder SGTA binding.
source: Because the interaction of Ubl4A with SGTA is mediated by positively-charged residues in Ubl4A including Lys48 (Chartron et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012), which happens to be the major ubiquitination site, the simplest model to explain reduced Bag6-SGTA interaction in USP13 knockdown cells is that ubiquitin conjugates on Ubl4A sterically hinder SGTA binding.
evidence: This is proposed as the simplest model based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: USP13 may serve an adaptor function to promote Bag6–SGTA interaction.
source: However, given that USP13 can also interact physically with Bag6, it is also possible that USP13 may serve an adaptor function to promote Bag6–SGTA interaction.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative possibility based on the physical interaction between USP13 and Bag6.

claim: The cleavage of Bag6 seems to occur within or near the C-terminal BAG domain based on molecular weight.
source: Based on the molecular weight, the cleavage seems to occur within or near the C-terminal BAG domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular weight of the cleaved product.

claim: The Bag6 co-factor Ubl4A binds to a site near the BAG domain.
source: It has been shown that the Bag6 co-factor Ubl4A binds to a site near the BAG domain (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Ubl4A normally covers a protease site in Bag6 either by itself or by recruiting a Bag6 cofactor.
source: Thus, it is possible that Ubl4A normally covers a protease site in Bag6 either by itself or by recruiting a Bag6 cofactor.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible mechanism based on the location of Ubl4A binding and the cleavage site.

claim: Hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A in USP13 knockdown cells may alter its function, leading to increased cleavage of Bag6.
source: Hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A in USP13 knockdown cells may alter its function, leading to increased cleavage of Bag6.
evidence: This is proposed as a mechanism based on the correlation between Ubl4A ubiquitination and Bag6 cleavage.

claim: Bag6* also accumulates in cells depleted of Ubl4A.
source: In support of this idea, Bag6* also accumulates in cells depleted of Ubl4A (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E) or cells expressing the Ub-Ubl4A fusion protein (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments in Ubl4A knockdown cells and cells expressing Ub-Ubl4A.

claim: Depletion of USP13 can impair Bag6 function via at least two ways: causing its cleavage and inhibiting its interaction with SGTA.
source: Our results suggest that depletion of USP13 can impair Bag6 function via at least two ways. One is to cause its cleavage and the other is to inhibit its interaction with SGTA (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the multiple phenotypes observed in USP13 knockdown cells.

claim: Increased cleavage of Bag6 may also contribute to reduced interaction with SGTA.
source: The two events may be linked as increased cleavage of Bag6 may also contribute to reduced interaction with SGTA.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible connection between the two observed phenotypes.

claim: Transient ubiquitination of Ubl4A by gp78 at the site of retrotranslocation may serve a positive role in ERAD.
source: Although hyper-ubiquitination of Ubl4A is clearly detrimental to ERAD, it is noteworthy that our results do not exclude the possibility that transient ubiquitination of Ubl4A by gp78 at the site of retrotranslocation may also serve a positive role in ERAD.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility that is not excluded by the current results.

claim: USP13 is required to antagonize a promiscuous activity of gp78 towards Ubl4A.
source: Because the accumulation of Bag6* upon USP13 depletion is significantly reduced in cells co-depleted of USP13 and gp78 (Figure 6D), we propose that USP13 is required to antagonize a promiscuous activity of gp78 towards Ubl4A, which would otherwise impair the function of the Bag6 complex by altering its interaction pattern and/or increasing its cleavage by a cellular protease.
evidence: This is proposed as a model based on the observation that co-depletion of gp78 rescues the Bag6 cleavage phenotype in USP13 knockdown cells.

claim: A DUB can cooperate with an E3 ligase to enhance its substrate specificity.
source: In this model, a DUB can cooperate with an E3 ligase to enhance its substrate specificity.
evidence: This is the main conceptual model proposed by the study.

claim: The specificity of a ubiquitination reaction has generally been thought to be controlled at the E3 ligase level.
source: The specificity of a ubiquitination reaction has generally been thought to be controlled at the E3 ligase level.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Many E3s appear to directly recognize substrates bearing degradation signals, leading to their ubiquitination.
source: In proteasomal degradation pathways, many E3s appear to directly recognize substrates bearing degradation signals, leading to their ubiquitination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: How E3 cofactors evade ubiquitination is completely unknown.
source: How these E3 cofactors evade ubiquitination is completely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Cooperation between an E3 ligase and an associated DUB may provide a solution that sharpens substrate specificity for the ligase.
source: Our study suggests that cooperation between an E3 ligase and an associated DUB may provide a simple solution that sharpens substrate specificity for the ligase.
evidence: This is the main conceptual contribution of the study.

claim: E3 ligases may ubiquitinate other factors that function in proximity in addition to substrates.
source: It is conceivable that while acting on substrates, E3 ligases may also ubiquitinate other factors that function in proximity.
evidence: This is proposed as a general principle based on the findings of the study.

claim: Undesired ubiquitination, even occurring at a low frequency, could cause significant damage overtime, particularly if it leads to irreversible inactivation of the modified proteins.
source: Such undesired ubiquitination, even occurring at a low frequency, could cause significant damage overtime, particularly if it leads to irreversible inactivation of the modified proteins.
evidence: This is proposed as a rationale for why DUB-mediated quality control of E3 activity would be important.

claim: Removal of unwanted ubiquitination products by DUBs ensures that only desired ubiquitination signals are maintained in cells.
source: Removal of these unwanted ubiquitination products by DUBs ensures that only desired ubiquitination signals are maintained in cells.
evidence: This is proposed as the function of DUBs in sharpening E3 specificity.

claim: Even non-specific DUB activities can amplify the specificity of a quality control E3, allowing discrimination between two misfolded substrates bearing subtle structural differences.
source: This concept is in line with a recent study, showing that even non-specific DUB activities can amplify the specificity of a quality control E3, allowing discrimination between two misfolded substrates bearing subtle structural differences (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Zhang et al., 2013 to support the proposed model.

claim: Lys48-linked ubiquitination can have a non-destructive function to regulate protein–protein interactions.
source: Our study also suggests that Lys48-linked ubiquitination can have a non-destructive function, which is to regulate protein–protein interactions.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion drawn from the observation that Ubl4A carries K48-linked ubiquitin chains but is stable.

claim: Cells can use ubiquitin to regulate protein–protein interaction in many ways.
source: Previous studies showed that cells can use ubiquitin to regulate protein–protein interaction in many ways.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The most common strategy for ubiquitin to regulate protein-protein interactions is to have ubiquitin serve as a 'signal' that recruits a downstream effector containing a ubiquitin-binding domain.
source: The most common strategy is to have ubiquitin serve as a 'signal' that recruits a downstream effector containing a ubiquitin-binding domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The regulation of Bag6 by the gp78-USP13-mediated ubiquitination cycle represents a paradigm where ubiquitination inhibits the recruitment of a co-factor.
source: By contrast, the regulation of Bag6 by the gp78-USP13-mediated ubiquitination cycle seems to represent another paradigm; Ubiquitination inhibits the recruitment of a co-factor.
evidence: This is proposed as a novel mechanism based on the findings of the study.

claim: A similar ubiquitin-dependent disassembly of a protein complex involved in TGFβ signaling has been reported.
source: It is noteworthy that a similar ubiquitin-dependent disassembly of a protein complex involved in TGFβ signaling has been reported (Dupont et al., 2012; Eichhorn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with references to Dupont et al., 2012 and Eichhorn et al., 2012.

claim: Ubiquitin conjugates on Ubl4A may be bound by one of the many ERAD factors that carry ubiquitin-binding motifs, preventing substrate recognition by the proteasome.
source: It is possible that ubiquitin conjugates on Ubl4A is bound by one of the many ERAD factors that carry ubiquitin-binding motifs (Xu et al., 2012). These interactions may prevent substrate recognition by the proteasome.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible mechanism for how Ubl4A escapes degradation despite carrying K48-linked ubiquitin chains.

claim: A similar mechanism has been reported to maintain the stability of the ubiquitinated transcription factor Met4 in yeast.
source: Such a mechanism has been reported to maintain the stability of the ubiquitinated transcription factor Met4 in yeast (Flick et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Flick et al., 2006 to support the proposed mechanism.

claim: The USP13 activity needs to be tightly regulated both spatially and temporally in cells.
source: Our model predicts that the USP13 activity needs to be tightly regulated both spatially and temporally in cells, a theme generally applicable to DUBs (Reyes-Turcu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is predicted based on the model and stated as a general principle for DUBs.

claim: Purified USP13 is inactive despite sequence homology to USP5, a constitutively active isopeptidase.
source: Indeed, we found that purified USP13 is inactive despite sequence homology to USP5, a constitutively active isopeptidase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the Ub-AFC cleavage assays.

claim: Sequence variations in a UBA domain allow USP13 to acquire new interactors, which may activate it at the ER membrane.
source: Our data suggest that sequence variations in a UBA domain allow USP13 to acquire new interactors, which may activate it at the ER membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the chimera experiments showing that the second UBA domain determines both activity and binding partners.

claim: Purified gp78 is insufficient to activate USP13.
source: Since purified gp78 is insufficient to activate USP13 (Liu, Y unpublished results), further experiments using gp78-containing retrotranslocation complexes reconstituted in proteoliposome are required to elucidate how USP13 is regulated in the context of retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished results.

claim: A ubiquitin ligase and a DUB can act in concert to coordinate protein turnover at the ER by regulating the ubiquitination status of a degradation machinery factor.
source: In summary, our study demonstrates that a ubiquitin ligase and a DUB can act in concert to coordinate protein turnover at the ER by regulating the ubiquitination status of a degradation machinery factor.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the findings of the study.

claim: An E3-DUB 'tag team' can enhance E3 specificity, a paradigm that may be applicable to other E3-DUB complexes.
source: In addition, our findings reveal a mechanism by which an E3-DUB 'tag team' can enhance E3 specificity, a paradigm that may be applicable to other E3-DUB complexes.
evidence: This is the main conceptual contribution of the study with broader implications.

claim: gp78 is homologous to Hrd1p, an ERAD-specific E3 in yeast.
source: gp78 is homologous to Hrd1p, an ERAD-specific E3 in yeast proposed to form a 'retrotranslocon' that channels misfolded proteins out of the ER (Carvalho et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Carvalho et al., 2010.

claim: Hrd1p is proposed to form a 'retrotranslocon' that channels misfolded proteins out of the ER.
source: gp78 is homologous to Hrd1p, an ERAD-specific E3 in yeast proposed to form a 'retrotranslocon' that channels misfolded proteins out of the ER (Carvalho et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Carvalho et al., 2010.

claim: gp78 forms a large membrane complex that communicates with machinery proteins on both sides of the membrane.
source: Similar to Hrd1p, gp78 also forms a large membrane complex that communicates with machinery proteins on both sides of the membrane (Zhong et al., 2004; Christianson et al., 2011), establishing it as a master regulator of retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is stated with references to Zhong et al., 2004 and Christianson et al., 2011.

claim: gp78 uses a VIM segment to bind p97/VCP.
source: In the cytosol, gp78 uses a VIM (VCP-interacting motif) segment to bind p97/VCP (Ballar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Ballar et al., 2006.

claim: gp78 has a CUE domain that recruits a multiprotein complex comprising Bag6 and its cofactors Ubl4A and Trc35.
source: In addition, it has a CUE (coupling ubiquitin to ER degradation) domain that recruits a multiprotein complex comprising Bag6 and its cofactors Ubl4A and Trc35 (Chen et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with references to Chen et al., 2006 and Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Bag6 contains an unusual chaperone 'holdase' activity, capable of maintaining retrotranslocated polypeptides in a soluble state to enhance their turnover.
source: Bag6 contains an unusual chaperone 'holdase' activity, capable of maintaining retrotranslocated polypeptides in a soluble state to enhance their turnover (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Bag6 was reported to interact transiently with the proteasome.
source: Moreover, Bag6 was reported to interact transiently with the proteasome (Minami et al., 2010), raising the possibility that it may facilitate substrate hand over from the gp78–p97 complex to the proteasome.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Minami et al., 2010.

claim: Bag6's 'holdase' activity can act in conjunction with other ubiquitin ligases to help degrade defective cytosolic and mislocalized proteins.
source: Importantly, this 'holdase' activity can also act in conjunction with other ubiquitin ligases to help degrade defective cytosolic and mislocalized proteins (Minami et al., 2010; Hessa et al., 2011), establishing Bag6 as a major E3-associated chaperone in protein quality control (Lee and Ye, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with references to Minami et al., 2010, Hessa et al., 2011, and Lee and Ye, 2013.

claim: Bag6 is a major E3-associated chaperone in protein quality control.
source: Importantly, this 'holdase' activity can also act in conjunction with other ubiquitin ligases to help degrade defective cytosolic and mislocalized proteins (Minami et al., 2010; Hessa et al., 2011), establishing Bag6 as a major E3-associated chaperone in protein quality control (Lee and Ye, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Lee and Ye, 2013.

claim: Many DUBs involved in ERAD associate with p97/VCP either directly or indirectly.
source: Many DUBs involved in ERAD associate with p97/VCP either directly or indirectly. These include YOD1 (Ernst et al., 2009), ataxin-3 (Wang et al., 2006; Zhong and Pittman, 2006), USP25 (Blount et al., 2012), USP13, USP50, and VCPIP1 (Sowa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Many p97-associated DUBs apparently serve as positive regulators in ERAD.
source: Interestingly, although deubiquitination has often been reported to cause removal of the proteasome targeting signals and therefore inhibition of protein turnover, many p97-associated DUBs apparently serve as positive regulators in ERAD (Wang et al., 2006; Ernst et al., 2009; Sowa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with references to Wang et al., 2006, Ernst et al., 2009, and Sowa et al., 2009.

claim: Experimental data in support of models explaining how DUBs positively regulate ERAD are lacking.
source: Several models have been proposed to explain these surprising findings, but experimental data in support of any of these models are lacking (Liu and Ye, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Liu and Ye, 2012.
